title: The Orphan of Makkah
subtitle: The Loss of His Mother and Grandfather
summary: The journey of Aminah to Yathrib with her young son, her passing at the desert outpost of al-Abwa', the profound tenderness and guardianship of 'Abd al-Muttalib, the grandfather's farewell, and the refuge found under divine care.

sections.text: Return to the Maternal Hearth in Makkah

Upon his return from the desert encampments of Banu Sa'd at approximately five years of age, the young Muhammad was reunited with his mother, Aminah bint Wahb, in the ancestral quarter of Banu Hashim. For a brief and tender season, the boy experienced the warm embrace of maternal love and domestic stability.

Aminah saw in her son the living reflection of her late husband 'Abdullah. His clear speech, polished manners, and resilient physical constitution—forged in the high breezes of the desert—brought deep consolation to her heart. Assisting her in his care was the devoted maiden Barakah (Umm Ayman), whose affectionate loyalty provided an unbroken thread of constancy throughout his childhood.
The ancient stone homes and winding alleys of pre-Islamic Makkah.
The Journey to the City of Ancestors

When Muhammad reached six years of age, Aminah resolved to undertake an ambitious journey northward to the oasis of Yathrib (later known as Madinah). Her purpose was twofold: to introduce her young son to his maternal kin among the Banu al-Najjar clan—the family of his great-grandmother Salma bint 'Amr—and to pay solitary homage at the grave of his father, 'Abdullah, who lay buried beneath its date palms.

Accompanied by Umm Ayman, mother and son set out on the long road of several hundred kilometres across the lava fields and dry valleys separating Makkah from Yathrib, a journey of many days under the sun of the Hijaz.
A Month of Memory in Yathrib

According to reports collected by Ibn Sa'd, they stayed in the house of al-Nabighah among Banu al-Najjar for about a month. The boy saw the date orchards and wells of the oasis, very different from the rocky hills of Makkah.

Reports transmitted by Ibn Sa'd, largely through al-Waqidi, relate that after the Hijrah the Prophet ﷺ recalled that visit: that he had learned to swim in the well of Banu 'Adiyy ibn al-Najjar, that he played with a girl named Unaysah, and that he pointed out the house where he and his mother had stayed and where his father's grave lay. These are sirah reports whose chains need individual evaluation.
A desolate desert highway passing through the rugged mountain gaps of the Hijaz.
The Parting at al-Abwa'
When the visit was over, Aminah set out with her son and Umm Ayman on the return journey to Makkah. At al-Abwa', a stopping place between Madinah and Makkah, she died.
The sources say little about her final illness. Most biographers state that the boy was about six years old, so that he had now lost both his father and his mother.

'Every living thing dies, every new thing wears out, and every great thing perishes. I am dying, but my memory will remain; I have left behind good and given birth to one who is pure.' — Rhymed words attributed to Aminah in later biographical works; the report's chain is weak
Aminah was buried at al-Abwa'. Umm Ayman brought the boy back to Makkah and delivered him to his grandfather, 'Abd al-Muttalib.
The Tenderness of 'Abd al-Muttalib
'Abd al-Muttalib, by then an old man, took the orphaned boy into his own care. Reports collected by Ibn Sa'd say that he showed him a tenderness he did not show even to his own sons.
Ibn Ishaq relates that a mat used to be spread for 'Abd al-Muttalib in the shade of the Ka'bah. His sons would sit around it until he came out, and none of them sat on it out of respect for him.
The sacred perimeter of the sanctuary framed by the stony heights of Makkah.

The young Muhammad would come and sit on it, and his uncles would take hold of him to move him back. 'Abd al-Muttalib would say: 'Leave my son alone, for by God he will have a great standing.' Then he would sit him beside him on the mat, stroke his back with his hand, and be pleased by what he saw him do. — Ibn Ishaq, in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham
Another Farewell: The Passing of the Chieftain

This period of his grandfather's care did not last long. When Muhammad was about eight years old, 'Abd al-Muttalib died. Reports of the old man's age vary widely, from about eighty to well over a hundred years.

Ibn Ishaq relates that 'Abd al-Muttalib had commended the boy to the care of Abu Talib ('Abd Manaf), who was 'Abdullah's full brother through both father and mother (Fatimah bint 'Amr al-Makhzumiyyah). Though Abu Talib had little wealth and a large household, he was known for his generosity, standing and loyalty.
'Abd al-Muttalib was buried at al-Hajun. A report collected by Ibn Sa'd relates that Umm Ayman saw the boy weeping behind his grandfather's bier.
'Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? And He found you lost and guided you? And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient?' — Surah Ad-Duha (Qur'an 93:6-8)

Abu Talib and his noble wife, Fatimah bint Asad, welcomed the orphan into their home, caring for him like their own flesh and blood. Through these successive trials of loss—fatherless before birth, motherless at six, and grandfatherless at eight—divine wisdom had stripped away every worldly dependency, cultivating within the young Muhammad a profound sensitivity to the suffering of the weak, an unshakeable inner resilience, and an absolute reliance upon the Lord of the heavens and the earth.
